name: Switch to Darce Configuration
summary: Switch to Darce Configuration begins with the bottom player's Buggy loop and seeks a separate head-and-arm grip when the armpit opens; reaching Darce Control/Top also requires establishing top control.
description: Learn Switch to Darce Configuration from bottom Buggy Choke. Seek an open darce arm path; top control is also required. Success: Beginner 30%, Intermediate 50%, Advanced 65%.
overview:
Within the buggy choke attack tree, this switch starts with the attacking player underneath side control, holding a same-side arm-and-leg loop around the top player's head and arm. Read the opponent's movement against that loop and check whether it opens the armpit-to-neck channel. The original control uses the raised leg, not a collar grip. Replacing it with a darce requires releasing the leg connection and establishing a separate arm enclosure through the accessible armpit and around the neck; an opponent's turn alone does not establish that new grip.

The darce configuration is mechanically distinct from the anaconda because the choking arm enters under the opponent's far armpit first and then wraps around the neck, whereas the anaconda wraps the neck first and connects under the armpit. This threading direction means the darce is favored when the opponent's far arm is elevated or posted wide, creating space under the armpit for arm insertion. The Buggy loop does not already supply that arm path: the raised leg must be released and the new head-and-arm enclosure established without assuming top control.

This transition depends on the opponent's arm position and the space their reaction actually creates. If the armpit stays closed, keep the Buggy loop and re-read the reaction. The darce configuration uses the attacking forearm and the opponent's trapped shoulder on opposite sides of the neck. Its grip does not by itself reverse the players: Darce Control/Top requires the former bottom player to establish top control as well. Sprawl and hip-walk details apply only after that top position has been reached, as a separate finishing continuation. If the opponent clears the loop and retains the pin, the attacker remains underneath side control.

attacker.name: Switch to Darce Configuration Attacker
attacker.description: How to execute Switch to Darce Configuration in BJJ. Attacking perspective with setup, execution steps, and counters.
attacker.overview:
The Switch to Darce Configuration begins from Buggy Choke bottom, with the attacker underneath side control and holding a same-side arm-and-leg loop around the opponent's head and arm. Read the top player's movement against the loop and check whether it opens the armpit-to-neck channel. Release the raised-leg connection only when a separate head-and-arm entry is available. The attacking arm must then find the accessible armpit and neck path; there is no collar grip to withdraw and no existing top ride to preserve.

The darce configuration is mechanically distinct from the anaconda because the choking arm enters under the opponent's far armpit first and then wraps around the neck, whereas the anaconda wraps the neck first and connects under the armpit. This threading direction means the darce is favored when the opponent's far arm is elevated or posted wide, creating space under the armpit for arm insertion. The Buggy loop does not already supply that arm path: the raised leg must be released and the new head-and-arm enclosure established without assuming top control.

This transition depends on the opponent's arm position and the space their reaction actually creates. If the armpit stays closed, keep the Buggy loop and re-read the reaction. The darce configuration uses the attacking forearm and the opponent's trapped shoulder on opposite sides of the neck. Its grip does not by itself reverse the players: Darce Control/Top requires the former bottom player to establish top control as well. Sprawl and hip-walk details apply only after that top position has been reached, as a separate finishing continuation. If the opponent clears the loop and retains the pin, the attacker remains underneath side control.
key_principles: Read the opponent's rotation toward the choking arm as the trigger to initiate the darce switch rather than forcing the original buggy choke angle
Release the Buggy leg connection only for an available head-and-arm entry, then redirect the arm through the exposed armpit and around the neck
Thread the choking arm under the opponent's far armpit first, then wrap around the back of the neck to establish the darce arm path
Lock the figure-four grip with the choking arm's hand gripping your own bicep and the support arm's hand pressing the opponent's head or trapped shoulder down
Maintain head-and-arm contact and protect inside space from underneath; a grip change alone does not provide chest-to-back pressure or top control
Use sprawl and hip-walk mechanics only after top Darce Control is separately established; they are not available from the bottom Buggy starting position
Prioritize threading depth over speed—a shallow darce grip that does not fully encircle the neck-armpit channel will not generate bilateral carotid compression
setup_requirements: Buggy Choke bottom control is established with a same-side arm-and-leg loop enclosing the top player's head and one arm
Opponent has begun rotating or turning toward the choking arm, exposing the far armpit and neck channel for darce arm threading
Bottom player retains head-and-arm contact and a usable body angle without surrendering all inside space as the leg connection opens
Opponent's far arm is elevated, posted, or separated from their body enough to allow threading under the far armpit
The opponent's near arm is positioned such that the darce threading path between neck and far arm is open for arm insertion

execution_steps.description: Feel how the top player moves against your Buggy loop and check whether their reaction exposes the armpit-to-neck channel. An elevated or posted arm may create access, but do not assume every turn supplies it. If the armpit stays closed, retain the Buggy loop from underneath and re-read the reaction.

execution_steps.action: Release leg connection and redirect arm
execution_steps.description: Open the arm connection to your raised leg without pulling the foot against the knee. Redirect the available arm toward the exposed armpit and neck while preserving useful head-and-arm contact. This replaces the bottom Buggy loop with a separate arm enclosure; it does not begin with a collar grip or a ride on the opponent's back.

Thread through the available armpit first and then around the neck, only while that path is open. Work toward enough depth for the forearm to reach the opposite side of the neck with an opposing arm inside the loop. The arm path must be established from your actual bottom-side angle rather than assumed from a turtle-top grip.

Use your support arm (the arm that was not threading) to cup the back of the opponent's head or press their trapped shoulder down, preventing them from posturing up or extracting their head from the darce channel. The opponent's near arm should be trapped between their own head and your choking arm, acting as the compression fulcrum.

Connect the figure-four by gripping your own bicep with the choking arm's hand while the support arm's hand presses the back of the opponent's head or their trapped shoulder firmly downward. Bring your elbows together to eliminate slack in the grip structure and confirm a separate head-and-arm enclosure before any finishing pressure.

Walk your hips toward the opponent's head and sprawl your legs back to create a perpendicular angle between your body and theirs. Drop your weight low against the mat and let gravity drive the compression downward through the figure-four structure. The opponent's own trapped shoulder provides the secondary compression point against the opposite carotid.

Squeeze your elbows together while maintaining the sprawl and hip angle to finish the darce choke. If the opponent defends by rolling to their back, follow them and maintain the grip—the darce finishes effectively from this angle as well. If the grip is not deep enough to finish, maintain darce control and work to improve arm depth before re-attempting the squeeze.

common_counters.counter: Opponent tucks chin hard and clamps far elbow tight to ribs, denying the armpit threading path during the redirect phase
common_counters.your_response: If the far armpit is blocked, keep the Buggy arm-and-leg loop and re-read the reaction from underneath side control before attempting a separate darce entry

common_counters.counter: Opponent extracts their near arm from the trapped position before the figure-four grip is secured, eliminating the compression fulcrum
common_counters.your_response: Without the trapped arm, do not treat the partial neck wrap as darce control. Retain or recover the Buggy loop only if its head-and-arm connection remains available, then re-read the opening

common_counters.counter: Opponent clears the head-and-arm enclosure during the grip transition and settles their weight back into side control
common_counters.your_response: Accept that the choke connection is lost and protect yourself with inside frames from bottom side control. Recover usable guard space before considering a new attack rather than chasing a neck that has already been freed

common_counters.counter: Opponent keeps the elbow tight and maintains top pressure, closing the space needed for the darce arm to thread
common_counters.your_response: Keep the Buggy loop while it remains available and wait for an actual opening. Do not attempt a snapdown or assume a top ride from underneath the opponent's pressure

common_errors.error: Abandoning the Buggy leg connection and all head-and-arm contact before the new threading path is available
common_errors.consequence: Opponent clears the loop and settles side-control pressure while the bottom player has neither the original Buggy enclosure nor a new darce grip
common_errors.correction: Confirm the armpit opening before releasing the leg connection, preserve useful contact during the arm change and keep inside space protected from underneath

common_errors.error: Attempting the darce switch when the opponent has not rotated and the far armpit remains closed
common_errors.consequence: The threading path does not exist, resulting in a shallow grip that cannot generate choking pressure and wasting the existing buggy choke position
common_errors.correction: Only initiate the darce switch when you feel genuine rotation toward your choking arm and the far arm is posted or elevated. If the opponent is static, maintain the buggy choke or wait for a defensive reaction

common_errors.error: Threading the choking arm too shallow under the far armpit without achieving full neck encirclement
common_errors.consequence: The grip cannot lock at the correct depth, creating a loose darce that the opponent easily defends by posturing up or stripping with minimal effort
common_errors.correction: Drive the choking arm deep under the far armpit until the forearm blade seats fully across the throat against the near-side carotid. Prioritize depth over speed for reliable finishing pressure

common_errors.error: Failing to keep the opponent's near arm trapped inside the darce channel during the transition
common_errors.consequence: Without the trapped arm acting as a compression fulcrum, the darce becomes a one-sided neck crank rather than a bilateral carotid choke, dramatically reducing finishing percentage
common_errors.correction: Keep the opposing arm enclosed beside the head while arranging the new grip. Verify that the arm remains inside the loop without assuming chest weight from a top position you have not reached

common_errors.error: Trying to apply a top sprawl finish while still underneath the opponent in the Buggy starting position
common_errors.consequence: The required top body angle is absent, and squeezing the arms cannot substitute for establishing the head-and-arm control and top position
common_errors.correction: Treat top control as a separate requirement before using sprawl and hip-walk mechanics; do not count a grip change from underneath as a completed positional reversal

common_errors.error: Releasing the Buggy arm-and-leg loop before confirming an available darce arm path
common_errors.consequence: The opponent can free the head and arm and restore the side-control pin before the new enclosure is established
common_errors.correction: Check the opening while retaining the Buggy loop, then coordinate leg release with the new arm entry. If the path stays shut, keep the original control and reassess

training_progressions.description: Practice with the attacking player underneath side control and the partner inside an unloaded Buggy arm-and-leg loop. Identify the available armpit before releasing the leg connection, then rehearse only the separate arm path. Drill 15-20 repetitions per side with pauses to check the starting role, knee support and new head-and-arm connection.

Partner provides light resistance and controlled movements from top side control. Practice reading whether the reaction actually opens the armpit for a darce entry while retaining the Buggy loop when it does not. Distinguish an accessible arm path from a closed elbow position without assuming that a turn has reversed the players.

Partner provides controlled reactions including elbow clamping, arm recovery and renewed side-control pressure. Practice retaining the Buggy loop when the darce path is closed and recovering inside frames when the loop is lost. Treat an established darce grip and a completed change to top control as separate checkpoints rather than importing a turtle-top attack chain.

Positional practice starts with the Buggy attacker underneath side control. The attacker reads the top player's defenses and checks the available arm path; the partner works to deny it and clear the original loop. Count Darce Control/Top only when both the head-and-arm enclosure and top position are actually established. A sprawl finish belongs after that positional change, not at the starting checkpoint.

flashcards.question: From buggy choke bottom, what opening should you check before attempting the darce switch?
flashcards.answer: Check whether the top player's reaction exposes an armpit-to-neck path with the arm sufficiently separated for threading. You begin underneath side control with a Buggy arm-and-leg loop, not a collar grip above a turtle. A turn alone is insufficient: if the path stays closed, retain the Buggy loop and re-read the reaction.

trap: Assume a top ride already exists

flashcards.question: What threading path makes the darce switch mechanically available?
flashcards.answer: The darce threads under the opponent's far armpit first and then wraps around the neck. Choose the darce when the opponent's far arm is elevated or posted wide, creating space under the armpit. If the far armpit is closed, keep the Buggy loop and re-read the opponent's reaction. The threading direction determines whether the darce is mechanically available.

plausible: Choose darce when near arm trapped

flashcards.question: They clamp the far elbow to their ribs as you thread for the darce—how do you adjust?
flashcards.answer: Keep the Buggy loop and re-read the opponent's reaction. The far elbow has closed the darce threading path, so retain control from underneath side control and reassess the opening before trying the switch again.

flashcards.question: Why must the choking arm thread deep under the far armpit before locking the figure-four?
flashcards.answer: Insufficient threading depth means the forearm blade does not seat fully across the throat against the near-side carotid artery. A shallow darce creates a loose grip where the opponent can posture up, create space between your forearm and their neck, or strip the grip entirely. Deep threading ensures the wrist bone and forearm blade create a tight seal across the carotid that cannot be relieved by head movement or posture changes.
flashcards.answer_line: Deep seal locks blade on carotid

flashcards.question: What role does the opponent's trapped near arm play in the darce choke mechanics?
flashcards.answer: The trapped near arm acts as a compression fulcrum. The choking arm compresses one carotid from the front, while the opponent's own trapped shoulder drives into the opposite carotid as the figure-four tightens. Without this trapped arm, the darce becomes a one-sided neck pressure that is far easier to defend and significantly less likely to produce a tap from bilateral blood restriction.

flashcards.question: From top darce control, how do you generate finishing pressure without arm strength alone?
flashcards.answer: Walk your hips toward the opponent's head while sprawling your legs back to create a perpendicular angle between your body and theirs. This uses body weight and gravity to drive the figure-four compression downward through the grip structure. The elbows squeeze together to eliminate slack, but the actual finishing force comes from the sprawl pressure and hip angle, not from bicep squeezing. This makes the choke sustainable and mechanically efficient.
flashcards.answer_line: Walk hips, sprawl legs, angle body

plausible: Squeeze biceps as hard as possible
Pull head down with the grip
trap: Lean back and yank the arm

flashcards.question: They clear the Buggy loop and settle side control during your grip change; what is your response?
flashcards.answer: Protect yourself with inside frames from bottom side control. The opponent has cleared the head-and-arm loop and retained the top pin, so neither a front headlock nor a top-position reset has been established for you. Recover usable guard space before beginning a new attack.

trap: Assume you are now in top guard

flashcards.question: What starting control and opening are needed for the darce switch from buggy choke bottom?
flashcards.answer: Start underneath side control with a same-side Buggy arm-and-leg loop around the opponent's head and arm. Their reaction must leave an accessible armpit-to-neck path while you retain useful contact. The switch requires a new arm enclosure; reaching the top Darce Control outcome additionally requires a real positional change.
flashcards.answer_line: Bottom Buggy loop; open armpit path

plausible: Only need opponent to turtle up
Far arm trapped tight to ribs

flashcards.question: Why coordinate release of the Buggy leg connection with the new darce arm entry?
flashcards.answer: Opening the leg connection before an arm path is available gives the top player room to free the head and restore side-control pressure. Check the opening first and preserve useful head-and-arm contact through the change. If the far armpit stays closed, retain the Buggy loop and reassess instead of abandoning it for an unavailable grip.
flashcards.answer_line: Keep contact through the grip change

plausible: Pause to confirm grip is secure

flashcards.question: Your darce is locked but they roll to their back to kill the sprawl finish—what do you adjust?
flashcards.answer: Follow the roll and maintain the darce grip throughout. The darce finishes effectively from the chest-to-chest position with the opponent on their back, and in some cases the finishing angle improves because gravity assists the compression. Walk your hips to maintain perpendicular pressure and continue squeezing. Do not release the grip to chase a top position—the darce is viable from multiple angles once the figure-four is fully locked.

plausible: Release grip to regain top position
trap: Abandon choke, pass to side control

attacker.safety_considerations: The darce choke is a blood choke that compresses both carotid arteries simultaneously, producing unconsciousness within seconds when properly applied. Always apply the grip progressively during training and allow adequate time for your partner to recognize the pressure and tap before the choke fully engages. The arm threading under the far armpit can strain the opponent's shoulder if forced aggressively, so thread smoothly rather than yanking. Partners should tap early when bilateral pressure is felt rather than waiting for vision changes. Practitioners with cervical spine issues should communicate this before drilling, as the head pressure component can aggravate existing neck conditions. Never apply cranking or twisting force—the darce is a squeeze, not a crank. Release immediately upon tap and monitor your partner for delayed symptoms after successful applications.

defender.name: Switch to Darce Configuration Defender
defender.description: How to defend against Switch to Darce Configuration in BJJ. Recognition cues, defensive options, and escape strategies.
defender.overview:
Defending the Switch to Darce Configuration starts on top in side control, with your head and an arm enclosed by the bottom player's Buggy loop. The grip transition begins when that player releases the connection to their raised leg and seeks a separate head-and-arm grip. Deny the threading path under the exposed armpit by keeping the elbow close to the ribs, and maintain a balanced top base while addressing the remaining neck enclosure. There is no collar grip or defensive turtle shell in the starting position.

The darce switch defense differs from a fresh entry because the bottom player already has head-and-arm contact through the Buggy loop. Top position does not make that choke harmless. Watch for the leg connection opening and the arm redirecting toward your armpit; act while there is space to recover the arm rather than waiting for the new figure-four to close. A partial release can leave the original neck restraint in place, so do not assume that a change of grip makes it safe to pull your head away.

Prevent the threading where possible, deny depth if the arm begins to enter, and recover the enclosed arm before the new grip is secured. If the head and arm are fully cleared, retain side-control position with safe frames and balance. If the Buggy loop remains, continue recognizing its choke threat. The attacker's darce grip alone does not reverse your top position; that positional change must actually occur before top sprawl pressure is available to them. Tap to a secured choke rather than relying on a late posture change.
key_principles: Recognize the release of the Buggy leg connection and the new arm path as the cue to deny the darce entry while the enclosure remains open
Clamp the far elbow tight to the ribs as the primary defense to deny the armpit threading path that the darce requires for arm insertion
Maintain a balanced top base with the head aligned and elbows compact to deny the arm path while the bottom player changes grips
Use the grip transition to clear the head and arm and retain side control, rather than sitting to guard as though you began underneath
If the darce arm begins threading, immediately work to extract the near arm from the trapped position to eliminate the compression fulcrum that makes the choke functional
Move toward the attacker rather than away when the darce begins locking, as turning into the choke reduces the choking angle and creates space for arm extraction
recognition_cues: The bottom player releases the arm connection to their raised leg and redirects that arm toward your exposed armpit, signaling a change from the Buggy loop to a separate head-and-arm grip
You feel the high leg connection loosen as the bottom player adjusts underneath you and reaches for the new arm path; your starting position is still top side control
The incoming hand probes beneath the accessible armpit before wrapping around the neck; this arm-first route distinguishes the darce enclosure from a neck-first anaconda entry
The arm-and-leg Buggy restraint begins to open while a new arm loop forms around the neck and trapped shoulder; neither a collar release nor a top turtle ride supplies this change

defensive_options.action: Clamp far elbow tight to ribs and tuck chin to deny the armpit threading path during the attacker's arm redirect phase
defensive_options.when_to_use: As the bottom player releases the Buggy leg connection and begins directing the arm toward your exposed armpit, before the new loop closes
defensive_options.if_successful: The new darce path is blocked and the attacker retains or recovers the original Buggy loop underneath you. You remain on top in the Buggy configuration, with the existing choke threat still requiring attention
defensive_options.risk: A late elbow clamp may fail after the arm has entered. Do not force posture against either secured neck enclosure; tap if the remaining space is gone

defensive_options.action: Clear the head-and-arm enclosure while the leg connection opens, then retain balanced side-control pressure with the neck free
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the bottom player opens the Buggy loop before establishing a new darce grip and enough space remains to recover the enclosed head and arm
defensive_options.if_successful: You retain top side control after the head and arm are free. The failed attacker remains underneath in Side Control/Bottom rather than following you into a guard-sitting escape
defensive_options.risk: A partially opened leg connection may still restrain the neck. Pulling away or forcing pressure before the whole enclosure is clear can tighten the remaining attack

defensive_options.action: Extract the trapped near arm by gripping your own wrist with your free hand and pulling the arm out of the darce channel before the figure-four locks
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker has already threaded under the far armpit but has not yet locked the figure-four grip. This is the last high-percentage defensive window before the darce fully consolidates
defensive_options.if_successful: Removing the trapped arm eliminates the compression fulcrum that makes the darce choke functional. The attacker loses the arm-in configuration and must reset to a different attack or control position
defensive_options.risk: Committing both hands to arm recovery can reduce your support on top. If the new figure-four closes before the arm is free, stop and tap rather than forcing the neck or shoulder through it

defensive_options.action: Keep the torso facing the bottom attacker while recovering the enclosed arm through available space, without turning the head independently
defensive_options.when_to_use: While the new arm loop is still shallow and you retain top position with room to move the head and shoulders together
defensive_options.if_successful: The head-and-arm connection opens and you stabilize top side control. This is retention of the top pin, not a recovery to bottom half guard
defensive_options.risk: Turning into a secured enclosure can tighten it. This response needs existing space and an unrestrained shoulder; do not turn through a locked choke

favorable_outcomes.how: Deny the new darce path by keeping the exposed elbow close to the ribs as the bottom player changes the leg connection. Maintain balance on top. If the attacker retains the Buggy loop, you remain its top defender; blocking the new grip does not itself clear the original choke.

Use the opening in the Buggy loop to free your head and arm before the new figure-four forms. Retain a balanced side-control pin only after the neck enclosure is clear. The attacker then remains underneath in Side Control/Bottom; no sit-to-guard movement or reversal is required for this counter.

common_errors.error: Freezing on top inside the Buggy loop and waiting to feel the darce lock before defending the new arm path
common_errors.consequence: The new head-and-arm grip can close before you recover the arm. If the attacker also gains top control, sprawl pressure becomes available; your original top position does not remove the choke threat
common_errors.correction: React to the leg-connection release and incoming arm while space remains. Deny the armpit path, recover the enclosed arm or clear the loop to retain side control rather than waiting for the figure-four

common_errors.error: Extending the far arm to post or base rather than clamping the elbow tight to the ribs during the threading phase
common_errors.consequence: The extended far arm creates a highway for the attacker's choking arm to thread under the armpit with maximum depth, making the darce grip significantly deeper and harder to escape once locked
common_errors.correction: Pull the far elbow tight against the ribs immediately when you sense the Buggy leg connection release. The elbow must seal the armpit gap before the attacker's hand reaches the far side of your body

common_errors.error: Pulling away from the darce by extending the neck and driving hips backward to create distance from the attacker
common_errors.consequence: Moving away from the choke actually opens the neck-armpit channel wider and allows the forearm blade to seat deeper across the carotid. Distance creation helps the attacker, not the defender
common_errors.correction: Move toward the attacker by turning into the choking arm and collapsing the space between your neck and their arm. Reducing the angle and space is the mechanically correct defensive direction for darce defense

common_errors.error: Attempting to strip the darce grip by pulling on the attacker's wrist or hand after the figure-four is locked
common_errors.consequence: The figure-four grip is extremely strong once locked and wrist-stripping wastes energy that should be directed toward positional escape. The grip's strength comes from structural leverage, not hand strength, making it nearly impossible to break with hand fighting alone
common_errors.correction: Focus on extracting the trapped near arm or changing body angle rather than attacking the grip itself. Arm extraction eliminates the choke mechanics entirely, while angle changes relieve pressure and create escape pathways

flashcards.question: On top inside the Buggy loop, what signals a darce switch and how should you respond?
flashcards.answer: The bottom player begins releasing the arm connection to their raised leg and directs the arm toward your exposed armpit. Keep that elbow close to the ribs to deny the new path while preserving a balanced top base. React before the separate head-and-arm loop closes; a collar release across your back is not the starting cue here.
flashcards.answer_line: Clamp far elbow to ribs instantly

plausible: Wait to confirm grip is locked
Turn head away from choking arm
trap: Pull head back to create space

flashcards.question: How can the Buggy-to-darce grip change let you retain top side control?
flashcards.answer: If the bottom player opens the original loop before the new grip closes, use the available space to recover the head and arm. Stabilize side control only after the neck is clear. You begin on top, so this response preserves the pin rather than sitting to guard; a partial release is not proof that the choke has gone.
flashcards.answer_line: Clear loop; retain top side control

plausible: Sit to guard with your neck caught

flashcards.question: They are threading under your far armpit but the figure-four is not locked—your best defense?
flashcards.answer: Extract the trapped near arm immediately by gripping your own wrist with your free hand and pulling the arm out of the darce channel. The near arm serves as the compression fulcrum that makes the darce a bilateral choke rather than a one-sided squeeze. Removing this arm before the figure-four locks eliminates the choke mechanics entirely, forcing the attacker to abandon the darce and seek a different position. This window closes permanently once the figure-four grip is secured.
flashcards.answer_line: Extract near arm, grip own wrist

plausible: Posture up to break the grip

flashcards.question: Why is pulling away from the darce counterproductive, and what should you do instead?
flashcards.answer: Pulling away opens the neck-armpit channel wider by stretching your neck away from your shoulder, allowing the attacker's forearm blade to seat deeper across the carotid. The correct response is to move toward the attacker by turning your torso into the choking arm and collapsing the distance between your neck and their arm. This reduces the perpendicular angle needed for effective compression and creates space for arm recovery while preserving top position.
flashcards.answer_line: Turn into the arm, close distance

plausible: Pull straight back to create space
trap: Yank neck away from the arm

flashcards.question: How does defending the darce switch from buggy choke differ from defending a standard darce entry?
flashcards.answer: You start on top with your head and an arm already enclosed by the bottom player's Buggy loop. Their change to a darce requires opening the raised-leg connection and building a different arm grip. That change may create an early defensive opportunity, but the original restraint can remain partly closed. Watch the actual enclosure instead of assuming a fixed time gap or that top position makes the neck safe.
flashcards.answer_line: Leg loop opens for a new arm grip

training_progressions.description: Partner begins underneath side control with an unloaded Buggy loop and rehearses the grip change at 25% speed. From top, identify the leg-connection release and the incoming arm, then close the exposed armpit with a compact elbow. Drill 20 repetitions per side, checking that the head remains free of finishing pressure and that neither player assumes a turtle starting position.

Partner rehearses the change from the bottom Buggy loop at 50% speed. Practice recovering the head and arm while the original connection opens, then retaining top side control. Alternate between denying the armpit entry and clearing an open loop according to the available space, without pulling against a secured neck.

Partner establishes partial darce threading at various depths. Practice near-arm extraction using the free hand grip on your own wrist. Build the full layered defensive sequence: first deny the armpit path, then recover the arm while the loop is open; retain side control only after the head is free, and stop if the enclosure is secured. Partner varies attack speed and commitment level to develop adaptive defensive responses.

Positional practice starts with the partner holding the Buggy loop underneath your side control. Defend the new arm entry while recognizing that the original choke may remain. Score for denying the darce path or clearing the loop and retaining top side control. Any later exchange after the partner actually gains Darce Control/Top begins from that new position, not an assumed turtle-bottom start.

variants_and_adaptations.description: The initial bottom Buggy control uses the same-side arm-and-leg loop in no-gi; it does not depend on collar access. The darce switch uses a gable grip or palm-to-palm connection rather than the classical figure-four, with the choking arm's wrist bone driving into the carotid. The no-gi version often requires faster execution because grips are less secure without fabric friction.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: No-gi practice after the Buggy leg connection opens and a separate darce arm path is available

variants_and_adaptations.description: After separately reaching top darce control over a turtled opponent, instead of finishing with a static sprawl, immediately roll the opponent to their back upon locking the figure-four. The rolling motion breaks the turtle base and places you chest-to-chest with the opponent on their back, where gravity assists the darce compression from a mounted angle.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: After reaching top control, when the opponent maintains a strong turtle base that resists top sprawl pressure, or when a fast finish is needed before they can process the grip change and implement escape movements

variants_and_adaptations.variant_name: Shallow darce to front headlock transition
variants_and_adaptations.description: From an independently established top head-and-arm position, when the darce threading achieves partial but insufficient depth to lock the figure-four for a finish, convert the position to a front headlock by walking to the opponent's head side. The partial arm threading provides neck control for snapdowns, guillotine attempts, or anaconda entries from the front headlock angle.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: After top head-and-arm access is established, when the far armpit threading is partially blocked and full darce depth cannot be achieved, but neck contact has been established

position_integration: The Switch to Darce Configuration begins with the Buggy holder underneath side control and seeks a separate head-and-arm enclosure. The arm-and-leg loop must change into an arm grip through an available armpit; it is not a collar-based turtle attack. The retained destination is Darce Control/Top, so both the new grip and an actual change to top control are required. Sprawl or roll-through finishing details belong after that destination is established. When the armpit stays closed, retain the Buggy loop and re-read the reaction. If the opponent clears the loop and preserves the pin, the attacker remains in Side Control/Bottom. Related front-headlock, crucifix or back-control entries have their own prerequisites and are not supplied by a failed switch.
conditions: Buggy Choke bottom control is established with the same-side arm-and-leg loop around the top player's head and arm
Opponent has begun rotating toward the choking arm, exposing the far armpit channel
Far arm is elevated or posted wide enough to allow threading under the armpit
Useful head-and-arm contact and inside space remain available from underneath while the leg connection changes
